video.title: 6 BORING Machines That Pay You Every Month (Ice, Water, Office Coffee)

summary: The video presents six recurring-revenue businesses built around machines that other businesses prefer to rent and have maintained: water coolers, scent diffusers, AEDs, ice machines, dishwashers, and coffee machines. It explains typical prices, equipment costs, servicing needs, and ways operators find customers, while using a narrated example of Harry adding several machines to businesses he already knew. The recurring model works when a small monthly bill solves a problem the customer does not want to manage. Its practical constraint for a solo founder is that sales, installation, restocking, and maintenance still involve substantial in-person work.

speakers.name: Harry
speakers.description: Narrates the video and the case study about an operator called Harry; the transcript does not establish whether that operator is the narrator.

ideas.name: Bottleless office water cooler rental
ideas.one_liner: Place plumbed, filtered water coolers in offices for a monthly fee that includes maintenance.
ideas.business_model: Monthly equipment rental and service fee.
ideas.customer: Offices, especially those still using bottled water jugs.
ideas.problem: The office wants cold, clean water without storing and lifting jugs or arranging repairs and filter changes.
ideas.offer: Install a bottleless cooler connected to the water line and handle filters, cleaning, and fixes.

pricing.model: Monthly rental per cooler, with price potentially adjusted for office size or headcount.
pricing.notes: The video says to price for customer size and avoid competing only on a low monthly price.

acquisition_channels.details: Walk into offices still stacking water jugs and offer to replace jug delivery with a bottleless cooler.
Start with building and office managers already known to the operator; one placement in a building can lead to another floor.

ideas.delivery: Buy and install the cooler, connect it to the water line, then replace filters, clean, and repair it. The video says filters are serviced about every six months.
unit_economics_claims: An installation costs about $1,000 to acquire the customer and install the machine; Quench's case cited about $1,100.
Filters cost $50 to $100 every six months or so.
A hypothetical 80 coolers at $50 per month would produce $4,000 in monthly fees.
The narrated operator says four coolers produced about $200 monthly by month two and 18 produced roughly $900 before filters by month six.
ideas.startup_cost: About $1,000 per placement including machine, installation, and finding the customer; Quench's case cited about $1,100.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Usually a few weeks to the first invoice.

acquisition.how: The described route depends on personal relationships and walking into offices. In-person sales are difficult to automate.

onboarding.how: A booking and contract process could be automated, but site checks, plumbing coordination, and installation need human work.

delivery.how: A person must install, clean, change filters, and repair a physical machine.

billing.how: Recurring invoices and payment collection can run through billing software, with occasional review for usage or price changes.

support.how: Service calls may be logged automatically, but repairs and filter changes require physical work.

uk_applicability.notes: The rental and service model transfers well. A UK operator would need to handle local plumbing and water-hygiene requirements.

risks: Filter usage can vary sharply by customer size; the operator says a large law office used filters twice as fast as a small dental lab at the same price.
Underpricing to win deals can leave the operator with barely profitable service work.
Installation and ongoing maintenance create a physical route that limits unattended operation.

quotes.text: The fee covers the filters, the cleaning, and the fixes. To the office manager, it's one small line on a monthly invoice.
quotes.speaker: Harry

quotes.text: Walk into an office still stacking jugs and offer to make the jugs disappear.
quotes.speaker: Harry

quotes.text: Smart operators sell better water, not cheaper water.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Commercial scent diffuser service
ideas.one_liner: Install a scent diffuser in a business and charge a recurring fee that covers fragrance refills.
ideas.business_model: Monthly service fee for a diffuser and fragrance replenishment.
ideas.customer: Hotels, gyms, salons, dental waiting rooms, and clothing boutiques.
ideas.problem: Businesses want to shape visitors' first impression with a consistent scent but do not want to manage the equipment and refills.
ideas.offer: Place a commercial diffuser and refill its oil regularly.

pricing.model: Monthly service fee, with the fee depending on space size and the number of units.
pricing.notes: Monthly oil cost is about $30 to $40 for a small unit and more for a large lobby; the margin is the difference between the fee and refill costs.

acquisition_channels.details: The video says salon owners, boutique owners, and other local businesses talk to one another and ask who provides the service.

ideas.delivery: Install the diffuser and refill it about once a month; the video describes serving a handful of local hosts on a route that can be run in an afternoon.
unit_economics_claims: A small diffuser costs about $150 to $250; a large HVAC-connected unit costs $600 to $2,500.
Oil for a small unit costs roughly $30 to $40 monthly.
The video describes a monthly route serving a handful of hosts.
ideas.startup_cost: About $150 to $250 for a small diffuser or $600 to $2,500 for a large HVAC-connected unit; other setup costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: The only described acquisition method is local business referrals, which depend on personal relationships.

onboarding.how: Scheduling and recurring agreements could be handled online, but fitting a unit requires a site visit.

delivery.how: A person must install the unit and physically replenish its oil.

billing.how: A recurring monthly charge can be collected automatically once the service agreement is set up.

support.how: Routine questions could be handled remotely, but a malfunction or empty unit requires a person to attend the site.

uk_applicability.notes: The customer types and service model are common in the UK; equipment and fragrance prices may differ.

risks: Revenue depends on retaining local hosts and completing regular refills.
A large unit requires more upfront capital, while oil costs and service time affect the margin.

quotes.text: A small commercial diffuser costs around $150 to $250. A big unit that ties into the air conditioning runs 600 to 2500.
quotes.speaker: Harry

quotes.text: Start with one salon or one waiting room, refill it once a month, and add the business next door.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Managed AED readiness program
ideas.one_liner: Charge a monthly fee to keep a customer's AED inspected, documented, supplied, and ready for use.
ideas.business_model: Monthly readiness subscription, with optional AED provision and CPR training.
ideas.customer: Gyms, churches, offices, youth sports clubs, and schools.
ideas.problem: AED pads and batteries expire, readiness needs to be checked and logged, and the host may need physician oversight.
ideas.offer: Provide an AED readiness plan, inspect and log the equipment, manage replacement parts, and optionally include the device and CPR training.

pricing.model: Monthly program fee, with different tiers for an existing AED, an included device, or CPR training.

price_points.label: starting price listed by other providers
another provider's program on a two-year contract
difference for the program with CPR classes

pricing.notes: The video says to sell the readiness plan, not merely the box, and describes CPR training as an add-on.

acquisition_channels.details: Approach gyms the operator already knows and offer a readiness plan.
The narrated operator placed units in gyms near the dental practice and churches attended by family.

ideas.delivery: Partner with a medical director, provide or maintain the AED, check and log readiness, manage expiring pads and batteries, and optionally arrange CPR training.
unit_economics_claims: New AEDs cost about $1,200 to $3,000; refurbished units cost about $600 to $1,200.
Replacement pads cost $30 to $80 and batteries cost $150 to $350.
The narrated operator says five refurbished units at about $1,000 each produced about $500 monthly and each check took about 10 minutes.
ideas.startup_cost: New AEDs are said to cost $1,200 to $3,000 and refurbished AEDs $600 to $1,200; the narrated operator paid about $1,000 per refurbished unit. Medical-director and other setup costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: The described sales process involves walking into gyms and using personal community ties.

onboarding.how: Forms, recurring schedules, and expiry reminders can be automated, but a site assessment and physician relationship need human coordination.

delivery.how: A person must inspect and log physical equipment, replace parts, and coordinate training or physician oversight.

billing.how: Monthly program billing can be automated once the customer and service tier are recorded.

support.how: Automated expiry alerts help, but equipment issues and readiness checks need a qualified human response.

uk_applicability.notes: The subscription concept transfers, but UK workplace and AED guidance, training expectations, and clinical oversight arrangements differ from US state rules.

risks: The video says rules differ by state and advises checking requirements before starting; equivalent UK requirements also need checking.
A medical director is part of the described program, adding a specialist dependency.
Expired or unready equipment creates serious safety and liability exposure.

ideas.name: Commercial ice machine rental
ideas.one_liner: Rent commercial ice machines to food businesses and include installation, cleaning, and repairs.
ideas.business_model: Monthly equipment rental and maintenance contract.
ideas.customer: Bars, restaurants, hotels, and other food-service businesses.
ideas.problem: If an ice machine fails, a restaurant may lose a critical part of its service; owners also want to avoid maintenance and cleaning.
ideas.offer: Place an ice machine and handle installation, regular cleaning, and repairs.

pricing.model: Monthly rental, varying by machine type and capacity.
pricing.notes: The cited monthly rental includes installation, cleaning, and repairs for Easy Ice; service scope and lease terms can differ by provider.

acquisition_channels.details: The video points to restaurant supply stores and refrigeration technicians as sources of leads.
The video says bar owners' group chats are another place to find leads.
The suggested first customer is a bar whose existing machine is limping along; word of mouth can support adding machines over time.

ideas.delivery: Arrange plumbing and refrigeration work for installation, then clean the machine about twice a year and handle repairs. The video says to hire a refrigeration technician and plumber.
unit_economics_claims: A new 500-pound modular machine costs about $3,800 to $7,000 for equipment.
Professional cleaning costs $150 to $300 per visit, twice a year.
The video estimates that a $210 modular rental leaves about $160 to $180 monthly before repairs.
A well-cleaned machine can last ten years or more; poor maintenance can reduce its life to four to six years.
The video gives a hypothetical 40 machines at $210 each as $8,400 monthly.
ideas.startup_cost: A new 500-pound modular machine costs about $3,800 to $7,000 for equipment; professional cleaning is about $150 to $300 per visit. Installation costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: Finding customers relies on trade relationships, local networking, and personal outreach to bars.

onboarding.how: Contracts and scheduling can be digitized, but plumbing, drainage, and site suitability need human inspection and coordination.

delivery.how: Installation, cleaning, and repair are physical tasks requiring tradespeople.

billing.how: Recurring lease payments can be automated after an agreement is signed.

support.how: Breakdowns require a technician and potentially urgent physical repairs.

uk_applicability.notes: Restaurants, bars, and equipment rental exist in the UK. Local plumbing, food hygiene, water, and inspection requirements need to be followed.

risks: Equipment failure can disrupt a bar or restaurant at a busy time.
Poor maintenance can shorten the machine's useful life and damage the economics.
The business needs reliable refrigeration and plumbing contractors and enough capital for equipment.

ideas.problem: Restaurants need reliable dishwashing and a regular supply of operating chemicals without managing separate equipment and supply vendors.
ideas.offer: Install or lease a commercial dishwasher, maintain it, and deliver chemicals on a schedule.

pricing.model: Monthly lease plus chemical orders, sometimes included up to a stated usage limit.

onboarding.how: Customer, usage, and delivery records can be digitized, but a site visit and trade installation are needed.

delivery.how: Equipment installation, maintenance, and chemical deliveries involve physical work.

billing.how: A fixed lease and scheduled chemical billing can be automated, with usage exceptions reviewed by a person.

support.how: Usage questions may be handled remotely, but equipment faults and supply problems require human service.

ideas.name: Office coffee service
ideas.one_liner: Place coffee equipment in offices and earn recurring revenue from beans and related supplies.
ideas.business_model: Place equipment for free or at low cost and earn margin on recurring coffee and consumable orders.
ideas.customer: Offices, especially those with around 20 or more employees.
ideas.problem: Office teams want convenient coffee without purchasing, maintaining, or restocking the equipment themselves.
ideas.offer: Place a brewer or bean-to-cup machine, supply beans and related consumables, and deliver on a recurring schedule.

pricing.model: Monthly service spend per employee or office, with recurring sales of beans and supplies.

price_points.label: larger office service spend can exceed this

pricing.notes: The video says machines are often placed for free because recurring bean sales pay for the equipment within the agreement. It recommends pricing per head rather than per machine.

acquisition_channels.details: Start with offices already renting a water cooler; the video says office managers refer one another.
The suggested cross-sell is to offer coffee to existing cooler customers in the same building.

ideas.delivery: Place a brewer or bean-to-cup machine, deliver beans and other supplies every two to four weeks, and upgrade the best accounts as they grow.
unit_economics_claims: A 40-person office brewing two gallons a day is said to use about 10 pounds of coffee a week.
At a 40% margin, the cited example estimates $108 weekly gross profit and over $5,500 annually from one break room.
Commercial brewers cost a few hundred dollars; bean-to-cup machines cost $4,000 to $12,000.
The narrated operator says two offices accepted coffee service in the same week and that coffee margin passed the cooler fee in the first month.
ideas.startup_cost: A commercial brewer costs a few hundred dollars; a bean-to-cup machine costs $4,000 to $12,000. The video says many operators place machines for free at qualifying offices.

acquisition.how: Existing customer records can identify cross-sell prospects, but the described sales process relies on office-manager relationships and referrals.

onboarding.how: Orders and account preferences can be captured online, but machine placement and site setup require a person.

delivery.how: Beans, cups, and other supplies must be physically stocked and delivered.

billing.how: Recurring invoices and per-head charges can be billed automatically, with account changes reviewed periodically.

support.how: Order questions can be handled digitally, but equipment faults and restocking issues require a person.

uk_applicability.notes: Office coffee service is a familiar UK business model. Supplier pricing, coffee preferences, and local delivery economics may differ.

risks: Machine placement ties up capital unless suppliers or customer agreements cover the equipment cost.
The operator must restock and service physical equipment on a reliable route.
Pricing per machine can miss revenue when office headcount grows; the video recommends pricing per head.

warnings.warning: Check local rules before installing or servicing water coolers; the transcript explicitly advises checking city rules.
Do not win water cooler deals only by promising the lowest price; the video says discounting trapped Quench salespeople at barely profitable prices.

quote.text: It worked. And it trapped them at a barely profitable price. Smart operators sell better water, not cheaper water.
quote.speaker: Harry

warnings.warning: Do not charge customers the same price when their filter consumption and service burden differ substantially.
AED programs involve expiring pads and batteries, readiness records, and physician oversight; check applicable rules and ensure the equipment remains ready.

quote.text: Somebody has to check it, log it, and have a doctor sign off on the program.
quote.speaker: Harry

warnings.warning: The video says AED rules differ by state and advises checking the rules before starting.
Ice machines require competent plumbing and refrigeration installation, and health inspectors check them; check local rules.
Poor maintenance can cut an ice machine's life to four to six years; regular cleaning is part of the economics.
Dishwasher installations require a plumber and electrician, and chemical deliveries need to stay on schedule.
Equipment businesses require physical visits for installation, maintenance, restocking, or repair, which limits how independently agents can run delivery.

lessons.lesson: Sell the outcome the customer wants, such as cold water or ice during service, rather than focusing on the machine itself.

quote.text: The office doesn't want a cooler. It wants cold water. The bar doesn't want an ice machine. It wants ice at 9:00 on a Friday night.
quote.speaker: Harry

lessons.lesson: A recurring fee works when it removes an ongoing task or failure risk the customer does not want to manage.

quote.text: Each one wins because a business would rather pay a small boring bill than own a problem.
quote.speaker: Harry

lessons.lesson: Sell on reliability and value instead of entering a race to the lowest price.

quote.text: Smart operators sell better water, not cheaper water.
quote.speaker: Harry

lessons.lesson: Price the service burden before placing equipment, taking customer size and consumable usage into account.

quote.text: The rule he wrote on a sticky note, price the visit before the machine goes in.
quote.speaker: Harry

lessons.lesson: Use the first customer in a building or existing account to create a path to adjacent customers and add-on services.

lessons.lesson: Maintenance is part of the product and affects how long an asset keeps earning.

quote.speaker: Harry

lessons.lesson: Look for businesses where the customer values uptime and wants to avoid owning a maintenance problem.
